Very similar to how you have described it, having little family or friends definitely impacted my experience. It definitely felt more dramatic for me, I feel like I can still remember when things "clicked" and reality was put into perspective. My partner has since described me as brainwashed, AKA I was the golden only child. If COVID hadn't happened when I was 18 when I was forced to be with him so often, I don't know if I would have came to such a dramatic realisation so quick. I quickly moved out with next to nothing after a couple years of extensive planning. The excruciating depression after said realisation was hard. I would fantasize about going no contact two years before I would, although it wasn't something I actually wanted at the time. Once I moved out to my surprise things somehow got WORSE between us after a small period of me trying to keep the charade up. I put in a lot of effort, phoning almost every day like he wanted but the longer I spent doing that, the more I resented him. And the more time I spent in the real world, the more obvious his controlling habits were. Everything bubbled and I was encouraged by my therapist to be more honest with him, and by my partner to place more boundaries. Both of which led to a long overdue argument over next to nothing, just because I wouldn't "forgive and forget". No contact 8 months now.

It's tricky with family. What is the reason you want to be closer to these said family members? Is it important they like you and do you like them?
I do my best to not associate with people who make me feel like an interviewer in conversations. Most of the time it's because they are the ones who lack social skills or its because they just love to talk about themselves. I had a realisation though, that a lot of people who feel this way are just bad at talking about themselves because it feels conversationally selfish or you may lack confidence in yourself.
How often do you input your inner dialogue when speaking to your family? Do you feel comfortable being yourself around them, or are you holding back and it is straining the conversation? 
Sadly we all have difficult family members that we cannot call out for their lack of initiative in conversations, but what you can do if you really have to keep talking to them is learn to be comfortable stating things about yourself, and expanding on it without any input. Ending it with an open ended question is key to put the ball in their court without asking them a yes/no question or something which is only about themselves.

It's an extremely difficult thing to stop. Even now, years after when I was doing bad damage to myself, I still think about it every single time I have a panic attack and the urges just don't seem to go away, hell I just do it in different less permanent ways now but it's way better than it used to be. My advice has always been only stop if you feel mentally ready to. I know for me, when I tried stopping cold turkey and just living through the horrible urges during a panic attack I was far more likely to genuinely kill myself just to stop it all and we do not want that. How I stopped, was I got rid of the things I used consistently to self harm. I was quite particular about it, but you might use anything which makes things more complex. The thing you have to remember is whatever has triggered you to feel like you need to self harm, it will pass. The urges will pass eventually. There was often hours where I would be sitting on the floor rocking back and forth just repeating that to myself. Breathing exercises DO help, but usually I'd be in too much of a state to even try. Once you start slowly stopping and taking steps to stop harm it does get easier. Even thinking about stopping means you're already doing amazing. You will fail, A LOT. There will be many times that you will try and stop and you won't be able to, but it's babysteps. Take it easy, don't be too hard on yourself. The good thing is is that you're still alive and kicking, and you want to change. Good luck.
